key_terms.meaning: Partial molar Gibbs energy of component i, μᵢ = (∂G/∂nᵢ) at fixed T, P and other n; at phase equilibrium it is equal in every phase present.
The 'corrected pressure' that replaces partial pressure in real systems, defined by μᵢ = μᵢ° + RT ln(fᵢ/fᵢ°); equal fugacity in all phases is the working form of phase equilibrium.
Ratio φᵢ = fᵢ/(yᵢP) in a vapour or fᵢ/(xᵢP) in a liquid; φᵢ → 1 as P → 0 for a gas.
Dimensionless fugacity ratio aᵢ = fᵢ/fᵢ°, where fᵢ° is the fugacity of the component in a chosen standard state, usually pure liquid at the same T and P.
All phases in contact share one temperature T and, across a flat interface, one pressure P; otherwise heat or volume flows and the state is not equilibrium.
A phase is stable only if its Gibbs energy is at a minimum, i.e. (∂²G/∂x²)T,P > 0; a negative curvature means the mixture splits into two phases.
A physically distinct and mechanically separable part of the system, such as one liquid layer, a vapour, or a solid crystal.
The smallest number of independent chemical species needed to describe the composition of every phase of the system.
The number of intensive variables (T, P, compositions) that can be fixed independently without changing the number of phases present.
F = C − π + 2, with C = number of components, π = number of phases, and 2 standing for temperature and pressure.

For a closed system made from known amounts of each species, fixing any two independent variables fixes the whole equilibrium state, including the phase amounts; when F = 1 at least one of the two must be extensive.
At a given liquid composition, the bubble point is the T (or P) at which the first vapour bubble appears; at a given vapour composition, the dew point is where the first liquid drop appears.
Plots of equilibrium pressure (or temperature) against liquid mole fraction x and vapour mole fraction y for a binary; the two curves meet only at pure components or at an azeotrope.
yᵢP = xᵢPᵢˢᵃᵗ, where Pᵢˢᵃᵗ is the pure-component vapour pressure at the same T; valid for ideal solutions and near-ideal components.
yᵢP = xᵢγᵢPᵢˢᵃᵗ, adding the liquid-phase activity coefficient γᵢ to correct for real-solution non-ideality in the liquid.
γᵢ = aᵢ/xᵢ; it measures how far the liquid mixture is from ideal, γᵢ = 1 meaning ideal and γᵢ > 1 meaning positive deviation from Raoult's law.
The slope of the solute fugacity against its own mole fraction in the limit xᵢ → 0: fᵢ = Hᵢxᵢ, with Hᵢ having units of pressure.
For high-pressure VLE both phases use one equation of state: yᵢφᵢ<sup>V</sup> = xᵢφᵢ<sup>L</sup>, so no activity coefficient appears.
Kᵢ = yᵢ/xᵢ, the ratio of mole fractions at equilibrium; for Raoult's law Kᵢ = Pᵢˢᵃᵗ/P and for modified Raoult's law Kᵢ = γᵢPᵢˢᵃᵗ/P.
A line joining the compositions of two phases that are in equilibrium with each other, for example the two liquid layers in extraction.

takeaways: At phase equilibrium every phase has the same T, the same P, and the same chemical potential (hence the same fugacity) for every component.
A phase exists only where the Gibbs energy is a minimum; a concave region of the Gibbs energy curve forces the mixture to split into two phases.
The phase rule F = C − π + 2 counts the intensive variables you may set freely; Duhem's theorem says a closed system of known make-up is fixed by two variables.
For a pure component the equality of chemical potentials reduces to equality of pure-phase fugacities, which defines the vapour-pressure curve.
Raoult's law yᵢP = xᵢPᵢˢᵃᵗ is the starting point for every VLE calculation; real systems need only γᵢ added.
In a very dilute solution the solute follows Henry's law fᵢ = Hᵢxᵢ, not Raoult's law, because its environment is solvent, not itself.
At high pressure the liquid is also compressible and non-ideal, so both phases are described by fugacity coefficients from an equation of state.
The same fugacity equality applied to two liquid phases gives liquid-liquid extraction; applied to a solid and a solution it gives the solubility curve.
bank_note: Long answers are built around the single fugacity-equality statement, then carried through the phase rule, Duhem's theorem, Raoult's and modified Raoult's law with bubble/dew calculations, Henry's law, and the high-pressure φ-φ and liquid-liquid/solid-liquid cases.

bank.q: State the conditions required for phase equilibrium between two phases of a multi-component system. Explain why equality of temperature and pressure is necessary, and why equality of chemical potential is the complete condition.
outline: Thermal equilibrium: no heat flow, so Tᵢ = T across phases.
Mechanical equilibrium: no work of volume change, so Pᵢ = P across phases.
For each component, dG = 0 at constant T and P gives μᵢ<sup>α</sup> = μᵢ<sup>β</sup> for every species i.
In fugacity form: fᵢ<sup>α</sup> = fᵢ<sup>β</sup>, which is what is actually used in calculations.
Mass transfer stops only when chemical potential is equal; T and P equality alone is not sufficient.
answer: The system. Two phases α and β of a C-component mixture sit inside one closed vessel that, as a whole, is isolated. Energy, volume and moles of every species can pass between the phases; the totals U, V and ni are fixed. At equilibrium the total entropy S = Sα + Sβ is at its maximum, so dS = 0 for every small exchange.

Thermal equilibrium. Pass energy dU from β to α at fixed volumes and moles: dS = (1/Tα − 1/Tβ) dUα. For dS = 0 with any dUα, Tα = Tβ. If Tβ were higher, heat would flow into α and S would rise, so the state was not equilibrium.

Mechanical equilibrium. Let the boundary move so α gains volume dVα: dS = (Pα/Tα − Pβ/Tβ) dVα. With equal temperatures this gives Pα = Pβ for a flat interface. (A curved interface carries a jump ΔP = 2σ/r, with σ the surface tension.)

Chemical equilibrium. With T and P equal, the convenient potential is G, which is a minimum at fixed T and P. Moving dni of species i from β to α changes it by dG = (μiα − μiβ) dniα. dG = 0 for any dniα needs μiα = μiβ for every i. If μiβ − μiα = 2.0 kJ/mol, moving 0.050 mol from β to α gives ΔG = −2.0 × 0.050 = −0.10 kJ = −100 J, so the transfer happens by itself: species move from high μ to low μ.

Working form. With μi = Γi(T) + RT ln f̂i, the term Γi depends on T only and cancels between phases at the same T, so the criterion becomes f̂iα = f̂iβ. For water over liquid water at 25 °C, the fugacity is about 3.17 kPa in both phases although the mole fraction is about 0.03 in the moist air above it and 1.0 in the liquid.

Why T and P are not enough. A beaker of pure water in a sealed flask of dry air at 25 °C and 1 atm has equal T and P everywhere, yet water evaporates until its fugacity in the gas reaches 3.17 kPa. A sugar crystal in an unsaturated syrup at the same T and P keeps dissolving. In both cases μ differs between the phases, so mass transfer continues.

Why μ equality completes the set. The three groups of conditions together make dS = 0 for every possible exchange: energy, volume and each species. For π phases they give (π − 1) temperature, (π − 1) pressure and C(π − 1) chemical-potential equalities, the equations that the phase rule subtracts from the unknowns.
Conclusion. Tα = Tβ, Pα = Pβ (flat interface) and μiα = μiβ for every component, written in practice as f̂iα = f̂iβ.

bank.q: Define fugacity, fugacity coefficient, activity and activity coefficient. Give the relation connecting them and state the standard states used for vapour and liquid phases.
outline: Fugacity fᵢ defined by μᵢ = μᵢ° + RT ln(fᵢ/fᵢ°); it has units of pressure and equals partial pressure as P → 0.
Fugacity coefficient φᵢ = fᵢ/(yᵢP) for vapour, fᵢ/(xᵢP) for liquid.
Activity aᵢ = fᵢ/fᵢ°; activity coefficient γᵢ = aᵢ/xᵢ.
Vapour standard state: ideal gas at 1 bar, giving fᵢ = φᵢyᵢP.
Liquid standard state: pure liquid at the same T and P, giving fᵢ = γᵢxᵢPᵢˢᵃᵗ after the Poynting correction is dropped.
answer: Fugacity. For a pure ideal gas dμ = RT d ln P at fixed T. For a real fluid the same form is kept by defining fugacity f through dμi = RT d ln f̂i (fixed T), with f̂i/(yiP) → 1 as P → 0. It has pressure units and acts as a corrected partial pressure. Integrating from a standard state: μi = μi° + RT ln(f̂i/fi°).

Fugacity coefficient. For a pure fluid φ = f/P; for component i in a gas mixture φ̂i = f̂i/(yiP). From an equation of state, ln φ = ∫₀ᴾ (Z − 1) dP/P at fixed T; φ = 1 for an ideal gas, and φ < 1 when attractions dominate.
Activity. ai = f̂i/fi°, the fugacity measured against the standard-state fugacity at the same T. Then μi = μi° + RT ln ai. It is dimensionless.
Activity coefficient. γi = ai/xi = f̂i/(xifi°). In an ideal solution γi = 1 and f̂i = xifi° (Lewis-Randall rule); γi > 1 is a positive deviation from Raoult's law, γi < 1 a negative one.

Standard states. Vapour: the pure ideal gas at T and 1 bar, so f° = 1 bar and the working form is f̂iV = yiφ̂iP. Liquid: pure liquid i at the system T and P (Lewis-Randall), so fi° = fi = φisatPisat exp[ViL(P − Pisat)/RT], which is close to Pisat at low pressure; the working form is f̂iL = xiγifi. For a dilute dissolved gas the Henry standard state fi° = Hi is used instead.

answer.text: Worked numbers (values from the Raoult's-law chapter: x₁ = 0.40, γ₁ = 1.540, P₁sat = 60.0 kPa at 343 K, P = 51.51 kPa, y₁ = 0.7177):

answer: Reading the table. The two fugacities are equal, which is the equilibrium condition. The activities differ because each phase uses its own standard state (pure liquid at 60.0 kPa against ideal gas at 1 bar); activity is meaningful only with its standard state stated.
Relation. f̂i = yiφ̂iP = xiγifi links all four quantities at equilibrium.

bank.q: State the Gibbs phase rule and Duhem's theorem. Explain the meaning of each term in F = C − π + 2 and show with examples why Duhem's theorem is more useful than the phase rule for a closed system.
outline: C = components, π = phases, 2 = temperature and pressure; F = degrees of freedom.
Examples: one-component two-phase gives F = 1; two-component two-phase gives F = 2.
Duhem: for a closed system of fixed overall composition, any two independent intensive variables fix the whole intensive state.
The phase rule counts only intensive variables; Duhem's theorem also fixes the phase amounts, because the material balances add as many equations as the phase amounts add unknowns.
A binary VLE flash is fully specified by T and P even though F = 2 and the compositions are unknown until the equations are solved.
answer: Phase rule. For a non-reacting system of C components in π phases at equilibrium, F = C − π + 2.

Terms. C is the smallest number of independent species that describe every phase (C = S − R − a for S species, R independent reactions and a extra constraints). π is the number of phases, each uniform and separable. The 2 is temperature and pressure. F is the number of intensive variables that can be changed independently without a phase appearing or vanishing.
Derivation. Unknowns: T, P and C − 1 mole fractions in each phase, 2 + π(C − 1). Equations: equal μi in every phase, C(π − 1). F = 2 + π(C − 1) − C(π − 1) = C − π + 2.

head: System
C
π
F
Meaning
rows: fix T and P; x and y follow

answer: Duhem's theorem. For a closed system made from known amounts of each species, the equilibrium state, intensive and extensive, is fixed by any two independent variables. When F ≥ 2 both may be intensive; when F = 1 at least one must be extensive; when F = 0 both must be extensive.
Why two. Duhem adds the π − 1 independent phase fractions as unknowns and the C − 1 independent material balances as equations: (C − π + 2) + (π − 1) − (C − 1) = 2, whatever C and π are.

Why it is more useful for a closed vessel. Benzene–toluene with z₁ = 0.40 at 373.15 K and 100 kPa: the phase rule only says that T and P fix x₁ = 0.2436 and y₁ = 0.4388. Duhem's theorem says the same two variables also fix the split: the lever rule gives 19.9 % liquid and 80.1 % vapour. That split is what a flash-drum designer needs.

An F = 1 case. A sealed 1 L vessel of water at 100 °C holds liquid and vapour at 101.3 kPa. T and P are not independent here, so they do not fix how much is liquid; the second variable must be extensive, such as the total mass of water charged.

bank.q: Draw and explain the P-x-y and T-x-y diagrams for an ideal binary mixture. Define bubble point and dew point, and use the lever rule to find the amounts of the two phases for benzene(1)–toluene(2) at 373.15 K (P₁<sup>sat</sup> = 180.1 kPa, P₂<sup>sat</sup> = 74.2 kPa) with z₁ = 0.40 at 100 kPa.
outline: Bubble-point curve gives P (or T) against liquid composition x; dew-point curve against vapour composition y.
At a given T, the bubble pressure is the higher curve on a P-x-y diagram; the dew pressure lies below it.
Two-phase region lies between the curves; tie line joins equilibrium x and y at the same T and P.
Lever rule: (amount of vapour)/(amount of liquid) = (z − x)/(y − z), with z the overall mole fraction.
Azeotrope where the curves touch: x = y, and no separation by simple distillation.
answer: Model. For an ideal liquid and an ideal-gas vapour, yiP = xiPisat. For a binary, the bubble line is P = x₁P₁sat + x₂P₂sat (straight in x₁) and the dew line is 1/P = y₁/P₁sat + y₂/P₂sat (curved, below the bubble line).

answer.text: P-x-y data for benzene(1)–toluene(2) at 373.15 K (P₁sat = 180.1 kPa, P₂sat = 74.2 kPa):

answer: Drawing the P-x-y diagram. Plot P against mole fraction. The straight bubble line joins 74.2 kPa at x₁ = 0 to 180.1 kPa at x₁ = 1; the dew line through the (y₁, P) points sags below it and meets it at the two ends. Above the bubble line is subcooled liquid, below the dew line superheated vapour, and between the lines two phases.

T-x-y diagram. At fixed P the order flips: the bubble line (saturated liquid) is the lower curve and the dew line (saturated vapour) the upper one, running from the boiling point of the light component (benzene, 80.1 °C at 1 atm) to that of the heavy one (toluene, 110.6 °C).

Bubble and dew points. The bubble point is the T or P at which the first bubble of vapour forms from a liquid of given x. The dew point is the T or P at which the first drop of liquid forms from a vapour of given y. For a mixture they differ; for a pure component they coincide.

Lever rule. A balance on n mol of feed of composition z₁ split into nL of liquid (x₁) and nV of vapour (y₁): nz₁ = nL x₁ + nV y₁ with n = nL + nV. So nL/n = (y₁ − z₁)/(y₁ − x₁) and nV/n = (z₁ − x₁)/(y₁ − x₁): each phase amount is the length of the opposite arm of the tie line.

Azeotropes. An ideal binary cannot form one unless P₁sat = P₂sat. In real systems with strong deviations the two lines touch at x₁ = y₁; there the tie line has zero length and simple distillation stops.

bank.q: State Henry's law and compare it with Raoult's law for the solute and the solvent in a dilute binary solution. Explain why the solvent obeys Raoult's law while the solute obeys Henry's law in the same solution.
outline: Henry: fᵢ = Hᵢxᵢ as xᵢ → 0, Hᵢ a constant with units of pressure.
Raoult: fᵢ = xᵢPᵢˢᵃᵗ, valid as xᵢ → 1.
Solvent molecules are surrounded mostly by solvent, so Raoult's law applies to the major component.
Solute molecules are surrounded by solvent, so their escaping tendency depends on solute-solvent forces, giving Hᵢ ≠ Pᵢˢᵃᵗ.
Both laws are limiting cases of the same fugacity-composition curve: slope Hᵢ at x → 0 and slope Pᵢˢᵃᵗ at x → 1.
answer: Henry's law. For a solute i at low concentration, f̂i = xiHi, or pi = xiHi at low pressure. Hi is the limiting slope of f̂i against xi as xi → 0; it has pressure units and depends on the solute, the solvent and T.
Raoult's law (Lewis-Randall). For the major component, f̂i = xifi ≈ xiPisat as xi → 1. The slope is the pure-liquid fugacity, the tangent to the real curve at xi = 1.

Why the two laws differ. A solvent molecule in a dilute solution is surrounded by its own kind, so it behaves as in the pure liquid and its fugacity is its pure value scaled by x. A solute molecule is surrounded by solvent; its tendency to escape is set by solute–solvent forces, which the pure solute never feels. So the slope at x → 0 is Hi, not Pisat.

Why they hold together. Gibbs-Duhem at fixed T and P, x₁ d ln f̂₁ + x₂ d ln f̂₂ = 0, links them. If the solute follows f̂₂ = x₂H₂ over a range, d ln f̂₂ = d ln x₂, so x₁ d ln f̂₁ = −x₂ d ln x₂ = −dx₂ = dx₁, giving d ln f̂₁ = d ln x₁ and f̂₁ = x₁f₁. Henry for the solute forces Raoult for the solvent over the same range.

answer.text: Numbers (curve with P₁sat = 60 kPa, H₁ = 90 kPa, ln γ₁ = A x₂² and A = ln 1.5 = 0.405):

answer: Reading the numbers. At x₁ = 0.02 Henry's law is within 2 %, while Raoult's law for the same dilute component is 32 % low. By x₁ = 0.05 Henry is already 4 % high, so the dilute range is narrow.

Standard states. The solvent uses the real pure liquid; the solute uses a hypothetical pure liquid with fugacity Hi. They are linked by γi∞ = Hi/Pisat = 90/60 = 1.5 in the example. For CO₂ at 3.0 bar over water (H = 1670 bar), xCO₂ = 1.80 × 10⁻³, while the water (x = 0.998) keeps practically its pure vapour pressure, 0.998 × 3.17 = 3.16 kPa at 298 K.

bank.q: An ideal binary liquid mixture of benzene (A) and toluene (B) is at 350 K. Antoine constants (ln P in kPa, T in °C): benzene 13.7819, 2726.81, 217.572; toluene 13.9320, 3056.96, 217.625. Calculate the bubble-point pressure and the vapour composition for x<sub>A</sub> = 0.4. Then calculate the dew-point pressure and the liquid composition for y<sub>A</sub> = 0.4.
outline: Use Antoine's equation to get P<sub>A</sub><sup>sat</sup> and P<sub>B</sub><sup>sat</sup> at 350 K = 76.85 °C, in the temperature and pressure units of the constants.
Bubble pressure: P = x<sub>A</sub> P<sub>A</sub>ˢᵃᵗ + x<sub>B</sub> P<sub>B</sub>ˢᵃᵗ.
Vapour composition: y<sub>A</sub> = x<sub>A</sub> P<sub>A</sub>ˢᵃᵗ / P.
Dew pressure: P = 1/(y<sub>A</sub>/P<sub>A</sub>ˢᵃᵗ + y<sub>B</sub>/P<sub>B</sub>ˢᵃᵗ).
Check that Σyᵢ = 1 and that the dew pressure is lower than the bubble pressure at the same T.
answer: Saturation pressures. T = 350 K = 76.85 °C.

answer.pre:
benzene: ln P<sub>A</sub><sup>sat</sup> = 13.7819 − 2726.81/(76.85 + 217.572) = 4.5203   P<sub>A</sub><sup>sat</sup> = 91.87 kPa
toluene: ln P<sub>B</sub><sup>sat</sup> = 13.9320 − 3056.96/(76.85 + 217.625) = 3.5509   P<sub>B</sub><sup>sat</sup> = 34.85 kPa

answer: Bubble point, xA = 0.4. Raoult's law for an ideal liquid and ideal-gas vapour: P = xAPAsat + xBPBsat = 0.4 × 91.87 + 0.6 × 34.85 = 36.75 + 20.91 = 57.65 kPa.
Vapour composition. yA = xAPAsat/P = 36.75/57.65 = 0.637, and yB = 20.91/57.65 = 0.363; Σy = 1.000.
Dew point, yA = 0.4. From xi = yiP/Pisat and Σxi = 1: 1/P = yA/PAsat + yB/PBsat = 0.4/91.87 + 0.6/34.85 = 0.004354 + 0.017218 = 0.021572 kPa⁻¹, so P = 46.36 kPa.
Liquid composition. xA = yAP/PAsat = 0.4 × 46.36/91.87 = 0.202, xB = 0.6 × 46.36/34.85 = 0.798; Σx = 1.000.

Checks. The dew pressure of the y = 0.4 vapour (46.36 kPa) is below the bubble pressure of the x = 0.4 liquid (57.65 kPa), as it must be: the dew line lies below the bubble line. Both lie between the pure vapour pressures, 34.85 and 91.87 kPa. The relative volatility αAB = 91.87/34.85 = 2.64, which is why the vapour is much richer in benzene than the liquid.

Assumptions. Ideal liquid (benzene and toluene are similar non-polar aromatics, so γ ≈ 1), ideal-gas vapour at about half an atmosphere, Poynting factor 1. The Antoine set must be used in its own units: here T in °C and P in kPa with natural logarithms; using K or log₁₀ would give nonsense.

bank.q: A binary liquid follows the two-parameter Margules equation, ln γ₁ = x₂²[A₁₂ + 2(A₂₁ − A₁₂)x₁] and ln γ₂ = x₁²[A₂₁ + 2(A₁₂ − A₂₁)x₂], with A₁₂ = 0.60 and A₂₁ = 1.00. At the system temperature P₁<sup>sat</sup> = 80.0 kPa and P₂<sup>sat</sup> = 50.0 kPa. Find the bubble pressure and vapour composition at x₁ = 0.30 by modified Raoult's law, and say whether the system has an azeotrope.
outline: Write ln γ₁ and ln γ₂ from the Margules constants A₁₂ and A₂₁.
Calculate γ₁ and γ₂ at the given x₁.
P = x₁γ₁P₁ˢᵃᵗ + x₂γ₂P₂ˢᵃᵗ.
y₁ = x₁γ₁P₁ˢᵃᵗ/P; check y₁ + y₂ = 1.
Comment that γᵢ > 1 raises P above the ideal value and can produce a minimum-boiling azeotrope.
answer: Model. ln γ₁ = x₂²[A₁₂ + 2(A₂₁ − A₁₂)x₁] and ln γ₂ = x₁²[A₂₁ + 2(A₁₂ − A₂₁)x₂], with A₁₂ = 0.60 and A₂₁ = 1.00. Their limits are ln γ₁∞ = A₁₂ and ln γ₂∞ = A₂₁.
Bubble pressure. Modified Raoult's law: P = x₁γ₁P₁sat + x₂γ₂P₂sat = 0.30 × 1.509 × 80.0 + 0.70 × 1.040 × 50.0 = 36.22 + 36.41 = 72.64 kPa.

Comparison with Raoult's law. The ideal bubble pressure is 0.30 × 80.0 + 0.70 × 50.0 = 59.0 kPa with y₁ = 24.0/59.0 = 0.407. Both γ are above 1, so the real pressure is 23 % higher: a positive deviation.

Azeotrope test. An azeotrope exists if α₁₂ = γ₁P₁sat/(γ₂P₂sat) passes through 1. At x₁ → 0, α₁₂ = e0.60 × 80/50 = 2.92; at x₁ → 1, α₁₂ = 80/(e1.00 × 50) = 0.589. It changes from above 1 to below 1, so there is an azeotrope. Solving α₁₂ = 1 gives x₁ = 0.792, with γ₁ = 1.055, γ₂ = 1.688 and P = γ₁P₁sat = 84.4 kPa, the highest pressure on the bubble curve: a maximum-pressure (minimum-boiling) azeotrope.

Steps in an exam. (1) write the model and check x₁ + x₂ = 1; (2) compute both γ at the given x; (3) sum the partial pressures; (4) divide for y and check Σy = 1; (5) compare with the ideal value and comment on the sign of the deviation.

bank.q: The solubility of carbon dioxide in water is required at 298 K and 5.0 bar CO₂ partial pressure, where Henry's constant is about 1670 bar. Calculate the mole fraction and the mass of CO₂ dissolved per kg of water, and explain how the solubility changes with temperature and pressure.
outline: Apply fᵢ = Hᵢxᵢ with fᵢ taken as the gas partial pressure at low pressure.
xᵢ = Pᵢ/Hᵢ; quote the mole fraction in ppm if small.
Solubility rises linearly with partial pressure (Henry's law).
Hᵢ increases with temperature for gases of low solubility, so solubility falls as T rises.
Note the assumption: ideal gas phase and negligible Poynting correction.
answer: Law. At low concentration f̂CO₂ = xCO₂HCO₂. At 5 bar the gas is close to ideal, so f̂ ≈ pCO₂ = 5.0 bar (the water vapour in the gas, about 0.03 bar, is neglected).
Mole fraction. xCO₂ = p/H = 5.0/1670 = 2.99 × 10⁻³, about 2990 ppm on a mole basis.

Per kg of water. Molality m = x/[(1 − x) × 0.018015 kg/mol] = 2.99 × 10⁻³/(0.997 × 0.018015) = 0.167 mol/kg, so 0.167 × 44.01 = 7.3 g of CO₂ per kg of water. At 3.0 bar the same calculation gives 0.0999 mol/kg (4.4 g/kg).

Pressure effect. x is proportional to p: raising the CO₂ partial pressure from 3.0 to 5.0 bar raises the dissolved amount by the same factor, 5/3. H itself changes only slightly with pressure, d ln H/dP = V̄∞/RT, because the partial molar volume of a dissolved gas is small (about 30–40 cm³/mol).

Temperature effect. d ln H/dT = (h̄V − h̄∞)/RT². For most gases in water, dissolving releases heat (h̄∞ < h̄V), so the right side is positive: H rises with T and the solubility falls. A warm bottle holds less CO₂ at the same pressure, so it fizzes out on opening; cold water holds more dissolved oxygen than warm water.

Assumptions. The solution is dilute (x well below 0.02), the gas is ideal at 5 bar, the Poynting correction is negligible, and CO₂ is treated as a molecular solute; the small fraction that reacts to form carbonic acid and bicarbonate is not included.
Answer. xCO₂ = 2.99 × 10⁻³ and about 7.3 g of CO₂ dissolves per kg of water at 298 K and 5.0 bar; solubility rises in proportion to the partial pressure and falls as temperature rises.

bank.q: A mixture of 30 mol % methane and 70 mol % n-butane is to be flashed at 300 K and 20 bar. Use Wilson K-values (methane T<sub>c</sub> = 190.6 K, P<sub>c</sub> = 45.99 bar, ω = 0.012; n-butane 425.1 K, 37.96 bar, 0.200) for the first pass, then outline the φ-φ calculation with a cubic equation of state, showing how the K-values are obtained and how the flash is converged.
outline: Choose an equation of state and mixing rules; get fugacity coefficients φᵢ from it.
Equilibrium: yᵢφᵢ<sup>V</sup> = xᵢφᵢ<sup>L</sup>, so Kᵢ = φᵢ<sup>L</sup>/φᵢ<sup>V</sup>.
Kᵢ depends on both compositions, so the calculation is iterative.
Rachford-Rice equation for the vapour fraction β, solved by Newton iteration.
Update compositions using new φ values; stop when successive K values agree within a small tolerance.
answer: First pass with Wilson K-values. Ki = (Pc,i/P) exp[5.373(1 + ωi)(1 − Tc,i/T)].
Phase test. ΣziKi = 0.30 × 16.70 + 0.70 × 0.129 = 5.10 > 1 and Σzi/Ki = 0.30/16.70 + 0.70/0.129 = 5.44 > 1, so the feed lies inside the two-phase region.

Binary shortcut. For two components x₁ + x₂ = 1 and K₁x₁ + K₂x₂ = 1 give x₁ = (1 − K₂)/(K₁ − K₂) = 0.871/16.57 = 0.0526 and y₁ = K₁x₁ = 0.878. The lever rule gives β = (z₁ − x₁)/(y₁ − x₁) = 0.2474/0.8253 = 0.300. The Rachford-Rice equation Σzi(Ki − 1)/[1 + β(Ki − 1)] = 0 gives the same β and is the general route for more components.

φ-φ equilibrium. yiφ̂iV = xiφ̂iL, so Ki = φ̂iL/φ̂iV. Both coefficients come from one cubic EOS (Peng-Robinson, say): ai and bi from Tc, Pc, ω; mixture a = ΣΣ xixj(1 − kij)√(aiaj) and b = Σxibi, once with x and once with y.

The loop. (1) With the current x and y, solve the cubic for Z: smallest root for the liquid, largest for the vapour. (2) Evaluate φ̂iL and φ̂iV from the EOS fugacity expression. (3) Update Ki = φ̂iL/φ̂iV. (4) Solve Rachford-Rice for β by Newton's method, starting between 0 and 1. (5) New xi = zi/[1 + β(Ki − 1)], yi = Kixi. (6) Repeat until Σ(ln Ki,new − ln Ki,old)² falls below about 10⁻¹⁰, or the fugacity ratios f̂iL/f̂iV all equal 1 within 10⁻⁶.

Pitfalls. Wilson K-values ignore composition and are only a starting point; the converged values for this mixture differ from them. Near the critical region the loop can converge to the trivial solution x = y, K = 1; reject it and restart. If Rachford-Rice has no root in 0 < β < 1, report a single phase.
First-pass result. β = 0.300, liquid 5.3 % methane, vapour 87.8 % methane: methane goes overhead, n-butane stays in the liquid.

bank.q: Two partially miscible liquids A and B have G<sup>E</sup>/RT = 2.5x<sub>A</sub>x<sub>B</sub> at 300 K. Using activity coefficients, set up the equations that give the compositions of the two coexisting liquid layers, solve them, and state how tie lines are drawn on a triangular diagram when a third component is added.
outline: Equilibrium condition for each component: xᵢ<sup>α</sup> γᵢ<sup>α</sup> = xᵢ<sup>β</sup> γᵢ<sup>β</sup>, since pure-component standard states cancel.
Two such equations (one per component) in the two unknown layer compositions; the symmetric model makes the layers mirror images.
Solution gives the binodal (coexistence) curve.
Tie lines join the two liquid compositions at equilibrium; they are not parallel in general.
Distribution coefficient Kᵢ = xᵢ<sup>β</sup>/xᵢ<sup>α</sup> = γᵢ<sup>α</sup>/γᵢ<sup>β</sup>; selectivity of extraction depends on it.
answer: Equilibrium conditions. Each component has equal fugacity in the two layers. With the same pure-liquid standard state in both, fi cancels and xiαγiα = xiβγiβ for i = A and B: two equations in the two unknowns xAα and xAβ.
Activity coefficients. GE/RT = 2.5xAxB gives ln γA = 2.5xB² and ln γB = 2.5xA². A single phase is unstable where 1/xA + 1/xB − 5 < 0, so the mixture must split.
Solving. The model is symmetric, so the layers are mirror images: xAα = x and xAβ = 1 − x. Dividing the two isoactivity equations and taking logs reduces both to ln[x/(1 − x)] + 2.5(1 − 2x) = 0.

Result and check. Layer α has xA = 0.145, layer β has xA = 0.855. Activity of A: layer α, 0.145 × exp(2.5 × 0.855²) = 0.145 × 6.22 = 0.902; layer β, 0.855 × exp(2.5 × 0.145²) = 0.855 × 1.054 = 0.901. Equal within rounding, and by symmetry the same holds for B.
Lever rule. A feed with zA = 0.40 splits into layers in the ratio n_α/n_β = (0.855 − 0.40)/(0.40 − 0.145) = 1.78, so 64 % of it forms the A-lean layer.

Adding a third component. On a triangular diagram each corner is a pure component. The two binary layer compositions sit on the A–B edge. Adding solute C, each pair of coexisting layers found from xiαγiα = xiβγiβ for all three components is plotted and joined by a tie line; the ends of all tie lines trace the binodal curve. Tie lines are generally not parallel: they slope toward the layer that takes more solute, with distribution coefficient KC = xCβ/xCα = γCα/γCβ. As more C is added the layers grow alike, the tie lines shorten, and they vanish at the plait point.

bank.q: Explain, with the Gibbs energy against composition curve, why a binary liquid mixture splits into two phases. Distinguish the binodal from the spinodal curve and state the stability condition. Illustrate with g<sup>M</sup>/RT = x₁ ln x₁ + x₂ ln x₂ + 2.5x₁x₂.
outline: Plot Gmix against x₁ at constant T and P; a concave region means (∂²G/∂x₁²) < 0.
A single phase with a concave curve would lower its G by splitting into two phases.
Common tangent to the two minima gives the binodal (phase boundary) compositions.
Spinodal is where the curvature is zero; inside it the mixture is unstable and splits spontaneously.
Between binodal and spinodal the state is metastable; nucleation is needed.
Limiting case of the critical solution point where the two curves meet.
answer: The curve. At fixed T and P a mixture takes the state with the lowest total G. For gM/RT = x₁ ln x₁ + x₂ ln x₂ + Ax₁x₂ the ideal terms are always negative and curve upward; the Ax₁x₂ term (A > 0, unlike molecules attract less) is positive and bends the middle upward.

Why it splits. The curve has two minima near x₁ = 0.145 and 0.855 and a hump at 0.5. An equimolar single phase has gM/RT = −0.068, but two layers of x₁ = 0.145 and 0.855 have −0.104 on average: splitting lowers G by 0.036RT = 90 J/mol at 300 K, so the single phase cannot persist.

Stability condition. A phase is stable to small changes only if (∂²gM/∂x₁²)T,P > 0, here 1/x₁ + 1/x₂ − 2A > 0. At x₁ = 0.5 it is 4 − 5 = −1 < 0 (unstable); at x₁ = 0.2 it is 5 + 1.25 − 5 = +1.25 > 0 (locally stable).

Binodal. The common tangent touching the curve at two points gives the compositions of the coexisting phases, because equal slopes and intercepts mean equal μ₁ and μ₂. Here x₁ = 0.145 and 0.855 (the symmetric model makes the tangent horizontal). Plotting these against T gives the binodal curve.
Spinodal. The locus of inflection points, ∂²gM/∂x₁² = 0: x₁(1 − x₁) = 1/(2A) = 0.2, so x₁ = 0.276 and 0.724.

Three regions. 0.145 < x₁ < 0.276 (and 0.724 to 0.855): metastable; the curvature is positive, so small fluctuations raise G and the phase splits only after a nucleus of the other phase forms. 0.276 < x₁ < 0.724: unstable; any small fluctuation lowers G and the mixture separates at once (spinodal decomposition). Outside 0.145 to 0.855: stable single phase.

Critical solution point. The minima merge when the spinodal roots meet at x₁ = 0.5, which needs 4 − 2A = 0, A = 2. If A = 750/T, A = 2.5 at 300 K and the split disappears above 375 K, the upper critical solution temperature, where binodal and spinodal touch.

bank.q: A binary system shows a minimum-boiling azeotrope. Explain how this follows from the activity coefficients, how the phase rule applies at the azeotrope, and why ordinary distillation cannot separate it. Illustrate with a system at 343 K that follows ln γ₁ = 1.2x₂² and ln γ₂ = 1.2x₁², with P₁<sup>sat</sup> = 60.0 kPa and P₂<sup>sat</sup> = 20.0 kPa.
outline: Azeotrope means xᵢ = yᵢ, so from modified Raoult's law γᵢPᵢˢᵃᵗ = P for each component.
A minimum-boiling azeotrope requires γᵢ > 1 (positive deviation from Raoult's law) and P above the ideal bubble pressure.
Binary VLE has F = 2 (C = 2, π = 2); the extra condition x₁ = y₁ removes one, so F = 1 and fixing T fixes P and the azeotropic composition.
At the azeotropic composition the vapour has the same composition as the liquid, so no enrichment occurs.
Use of a different solvent, pressure-swing or azeotropic distillation is needed.
Mention the Gibbs-Duhem consistency test on measured γ values before trusting the conclusion.
answer: From modified Raoult's law. yiP = xiγiPisat. At an azeotrope xi = yi, so P = γ₁P₁sat = γ₂P₂sat and γ₁/γ₂ = P₂sat/P₁sat.

Why positive deviation gives a minimum-boiling azeotrope. With γi > 1 the total pressure rises above the straight Raoult line. If the bulge is big enough relative to the gap between the vapour pressures, the bubble curve passes through a maximum in P at fixed T, which is a minimum in T at fixed P. At that extremum dP/dx₁ = 0, and by Gibbs-Duhem the extremum is exactly where x₁ = y₁.

answer.text: Worked system (343 K, ln γ₁ = 1.2x₂², ln γ₂ = 1.2x₁², P₁sat = 60.0 kPa, P₂sat = 20.0 kPa):

answer: Reading the result. 60.13 kPa is above P₁sat = 60.0 kPa, so it is the highest pressure on the isotherm: a maximum-pressure, minimum-boiling azeotrope at x₁ = 0.958. Because γ₂∞ = e1.2 = 3.32 is large but P₁sat is three times P₂sat, the azeotrope sits close to pure 1 and is weak. At x₁ = 0.40 the same system gives P = 51.51 kPa against 36.0 kPa for ideal Raoult's law.

Phase rule at the azeotrope. Binary VLE has C = 2, π = 2, so F = 2. The azeotrope adds the condition x₁ = y₁, leaving one degree of freedom: at fixed T the azeotropic P and composition are fixed. Changing the pressure moves the azeotrope; ethanol–water at 1 atm boils at about 78 °C with about 89 mol % ethanol, and the composition shifts at lower pressure.

Why ordinary distillation stops there. Distillation needs y₁ ≠ x₁ on each stage. At the azeotrope α₁₂ = 1; the tie line has zero length and the lever rule is 0/0. A column fed on one side reaches the azeotrope at the top (minimum boiling) and cannot cross it.

Ways around it. Pressure-swing distillation (two columns at different pressures, where the azeotrope composition differs), azeotropic distillation with an entrainer that forms a heterogeneous azeotrope, extractive distillation with a heavy solvent that changes the γ ratio, or membranes.
Data check. The γ values behind such a conclusion should pass a Gibbs-Duhem consistency test before they are trusted.

bank.q: Compare the γ-φ and φ-φ approaches to vapour-liquid equilibrium. For each approach, state the assumptions, the data required, the typical pressure range, and the kind of system where it fails.
outline: γ-φ: yᵢφᵢ<sup>V</sup> P = xᵢγᵢPᵢˢᵃᵗ, with φᵢ<sup>V</sup> from a virial-type correlation and γᵢ from a liquid model.
γ-φ suits low to moderate pressure (roughly up to 10 bar) where the vapour is nearly ideal and the liquid standard state is well defined.
φ-φ: yᵢφᵢ<sup>V</sup> = xᵢφᵢ<sup>L</sup>, both coefficients from the same cubic equation of state with mixing rules.
φ-φ suits high pressure and supercritical components, where no pure liquid vapour pressure exists.
Failure of γ-φ: near the critical point, at very high pressure, and for supercritical gases.
Failure of φ-φ: polar and associating liquids near atmospheric pressure, where simple cubic equations give poor liquid densities.
Both reduce to the same fugacity-equality criterion of phase equilibrium.
answer: Common starting point. f̂iV = f̂iL for every component. The two methods differ only in how the liquid fugacity is written.

γ-φ (modified Raoult) method. yiφ̂iP = xiγifi, with fi = φisatPisat × Poynting. At low pressure this reduces to yiP = xiγiPisat. φ̂i comes from a virial correlation; γi from a liquid model such as Margules, van Laar, Wilson, NRTL or UNIQUAC.
φ-φ method. yiφ̂iV = xiφ̂iL, both coefficients from one cubic EOS (Soave-Redlich-Kwong or Peng-Robinson) with mixing rules and fitted kij; Ki = φ̂iL/φ̂iV.

head: Item
γ-φ
φ-φ
rows: liquid standard state is pure liquid at T; γ independent of P
one EOS describes both phases accurately
Antoine constants, γ-model constants from VLE data, virial B
T<sub>c</sub>, P<sub>c</sub>, ω for each component, k<sub>ij</sub>
low to moderate (up to about 10 bar)
hydrocarbons, light gases, CO₂, supercritical components
supercritical components (no P<sup>sat</sup>), near the critical region
polar and associating liquids with simple mixing rules
breaks down: liquid and vapour treated differently
continuous: both phases from the same equation

answer: Example where γ-φ fails. Methane–n-butane at 300 K and 20 bar: methane (Tc = 190.6 K) is far above its critical temperature, so it has no Psat and no pure-liquid standard state. The φ-φ route, starting from Wilson K-values (Kmethane = 16.7), handles it directly.

Example where γ-φ is better. Ethanol–water at 1 atm: the strong hydrogen bonding gives activity coefficients well above 1 and a minimum-boiling azeotrope; Wilson or NRTL fits these data well, while a simple cubic EOS with a single kij gives poor liquid densities and γ values.

Practical choice. Use γ-φ for low-pressure chemical systems with polar liquids, and φ-φ for gas processing, refinery light ends and high-pressure separations. Modern practice joins them by putting a GE model inside the EOS mixing rule, but both still rest on the same fugacity equality.

bank.q: Duhem's theorem is stated for a closed system. Discuss how the intensive state of a vapour-liquid-liquid three-phase system is determined, and how the phase rule count and Duhem's theorem are reconciled.
outline: Write the phase rule for C = 2, π = 3: F = 2 − 3 + 2 = 1.
Fixing T (say) fixes P and all three phase compositions, but not how much of each phase is present.
Count: 5 intensive unknowns (T, P and one mole fraction per phase) against C(π − 1) = 4 equalities of chemical potential.
Duhem adds π − 1 = 2 phase fractions and C − 1 = 1 material balance, leaving 2 variables; since only one may be intensive, the second must be extensive (total volume, heat added or a phase amount).
At fixed P the three-phase state exists at a single temperature; heat added there only changes the phase amounts until one phase disappears, as in boiling a pure liquid.
answer: Phase rule count. A binary (C = 2) with two liquids and a vapour (π = 3): F = C − π + 2 = 1. Intensive unknowns are T, P and one mole fraction in each phase (x₁L1, x₁L2, y₁), five in all; the chemical-potential equalities number C(π − 1) = 4, so one is free.

What one free variable means. Fix T and the three-phase pressure and all three compositions are fixed; fix P instead and the three-phase temperature is fixed. At fixed P the three-phase state is a single temperature, a horizontal line on the T-x-y diagram.

Duhem's count. In a closed vessel charged with known amounts, add the π − 1 = 2 independent phase fractions as unknowns and the C − 1 = 1 independent material balance as an equation: 5 + 2 − 4 − 1 = 2 variables must be fixed.

Reconciling the two. Duhem says two independent variables fix the state; the phase rule says only one of them can be intensive, because T and P are tied together here. The second must be extensive: the total volume, the heat added or the amount of one phase. Fixing T and P together is not two independent specifications in a three-phase binary.

Physical picture. Heat a vessel holding the three phases at fixed P: T stays at the three-phase value while one liquid layer is used up, exactly as a pure liquid boils at one temperature; the added heat changes only the phase amounts. When a phase disappears, π = 2, F = 2 and T can rise again.

Immiscible-liquid case. If the two liquids are practically insoluble in each other, each liquid layer is nearly pure, so f̂i = Pisat in its own layer and P = P₁sat + P₂sat. For example, if at some T the pure vapour pressures are 62 kPa and 40 kPa, the three-phase pressure is 102 kPa, so the mixture boils below either pure liquid at about 1 atm. This is the basis of steam distillation and of heteroazeotropic drying of solvents.
Conclusion. The phase rule fixes how many intensive variables are free (one); Duhem's theorem adds that a closed system still needs two specifications in total, one of them extensive.

bank.q: Solid A dissolves in liquid B. Derive the expression for the solubility of A in B from the fugacity-equality condition, and discuss why solubility rises with temperature when the heat of fusion is positive. Illustrate with T<sub>m</sub> = 330 K and Δh<sub>fus</sub> = 20.0 kJ/mol.
outline: Equilibrium: f<sub>A</sub><sup>solid</sup> = f<sub>A</sub><sup>solution</sup>.
Solid fugacity from the pure solid; solution fugacity written as γ<sub>A</sub> x<sub>A</sub> f<sub>A</sub>° with f<sub>A</sub>° the pure subcooled liquid.
Integrate the Gibbs-Helmholtz relation from the melting point T<sub>m</sub>: ln(γ<sub>A</sub> x<sub>A</sub>) ≈ −(ΔH<sub>fus</sub>/R)(1/T − 1/T<sub>m</sub>).
For an ideal solution (γ<sub>A</sub> = 1) this gives ln x<sub>A</sub> = −(ΔH<sub>fus</sub>/R)(1/T − 1/T<sub>m</sub>).
With ΔH<sub>fus</sub> > 0 the right side becomes less negative as T rises, so x<sub>A</sub> increases with temperature.
Activity coefficient corrections matter for polar solutes and non-ideal solvents.
answer: Equilibrium condition. Pure solid A is in contact with a liquid solution, so fAS = f̂AL = xAγAfAL, where fAL is the fugacity of pure liquid A at the same T and P. Below the melting point that pure liquid is subcooled, a hypothetical but well-defined reference. Hence xAγA = fAS/fAL.
The fugacity ratio. RT ln(fAS/fAL) = gAS − gAL = −Δgfus(T), the Gibbs energy of melting at T.

Path for Δgfus. Heat the solid from T to Tm, melt it at Tm (where Δgfus = 0), cool the liquid back to T. With ΔCp ≈ 0, Δhfus is constant and Δsfus = Δhfus/Tm, so Δgfus(T) = Δhfus − TΔhfus/Tm = Δhfus(1 − T/Tm).

Result. ln(xAγA) = −Δgfus/RT = −(Δhfus/R)(1/T − 1/Tm). For an ideal solution (γA = 1): ln xA = −(Δhfus/R)(1/T − 1/Tm), the ideal solubility, which depends only on the solute's melting properties and not on the solvent.

Why solubility rises with T. With Δhfus > 0 and T < Tm, the bracket 1/T − 1/Tm is positive and shrinks as T rises, so the right side becomes less negative and xA increases, reaching 1 at T = Tm. Physically, melting absorbs heat, so by Le Chatelier's principle warming favours the liquid (dissolved) state. A larger Δhfus makes the curve steeper, and the table shows xA rising from 0.37 to 0.80 between 290 and 320 K.

Limits. The result holds for T < Tm with a pure solid phase; it neglects ΔCp (less accurate far below Tm) and solid-solid transitions. A non-ideal solvent with γA > 1 lowers the solubility (0.268 instead of 0.482 at γA = 1.8). Writing the same equation for B and solving xA + xB = 1 gives the eutectic.

glossary.def: A state in which every phase has the same temperature and pressure and every component has the same chemical potential in every phase, so no net transfer occurs.
The partial molar Gibbs energy of a component, equal to the rate of change of the total Gibbs energy per mole of that component added, at constant T, P and amounts of the others.
A pseudo-pressure that makes the ideal-gas chemical potential formula work for real fluids.
The ratio of a component's fugacity to its partial pressure, equal to 1 for an ideal gas.
The dimensionless ratio of a component's fugacity to its value in a chosen standard state.
The factor by which a component's behaviour in a mixture differs from ideal, equal to activity divided by mole fraction.
A solution in which every component obeys Raoult's law over the whole composition range and the heat of mixing is zero.
A defined reference state at the same temperature and pressure as the system, used to measure fugacity and activity; pure liquid is usual for liquids and ideal gas at 1 bar for vapours.
The relation F = C − π + 2 giving the number of intensive variables that can be set independently.
An independent chemical species needed to define the composition of all phases in the system.
One intensive variable that can be changed independently without changing the number of phases in equilibrium.
The statement that in a closed system made from known amounts of each species, any two independent variables fix the entire equilibrium state.
The temperature or pressure at which the first bubble of vapour forms in a liquid of given composition.
The temperature or pressure at which the first drop of liquid forms in a vapour of given composition.
A mixture whose liquid and vapour compositions are identical at equilibrium, so simple distillation cannot change its composition.
The ratio K₁/K₂ of the K-values of two components, which measures how easily they can be separated.
The relation yᵢP = xᵢPᵢˢᵃᵗ that describes vapour-liquid equilibrium for ideal solutions.
The relation that the solute fugacity in a very dilute solution is proportional to the solute mole fraction, with Henry's constant as the proportionality.
The slope of solute fugacity against solute mole fraction at infinite dilution, having units of pressure.
A mass-balance rule giving the relative amounts of two coexisting phases from the distances of the overall composition from the two phase compositions on a tie line.
A line joining the compositions of two phases that are in equilibrium with each other.
The boundary curve on a phase diagram, given by the common tangent construction, separating one-phase from two-phase behaviour.
The locus where the second derivative of Gibbs energy with composition is zero, marking the limit of spontaneous phase splitting.
The equilibrium ratio of the mole fractions of a component in two coexisting phases.
A small exponential factor that corrects liquid fugacity for pressure difference from the saturation pressure, usually near 1 at low pressure.
